summary:
Earth as a Testing Ground for Moon and Mars Bases

NASA has a new base prototype for the Moon or Mars and needs to test it. That doesn’t require leaving Earth, because some places here have conditions very close to lunar and Martian ones. Our website collects them.

We picked sites that resemble the Moon and Mars in geology, terrain, and survival conditions, and put them on an interactive map. Click a location and the site shows how it compares with Mars or the Moon, so you can check the similarity yourself.

The main idea of the project is to let scientists find suitable places in one click instead of piecing them together from scattered sources.

Why our website?

Scientific facts are presented simply and visually, so they’re easy to take in. The map and comparisons let you explore on your own, which beats reading a textbook. Children like the bright visuals and get curious about science. Adults and specialists get the data itself. A suitable place is quick to find, and its comparison with the Moon and Mars is right there.
details:
Our project is an interactive guide to places on Earth that resemble the Moon and Mars. It helps test NASA base prototypes in conditions close to lunar and Martian ones.

How it works. We selected sites that are close to the Moon and Mars in geology, terrain, and survival conditions, and marked them on a map. Click any location and the site shows how it compares with the Moon or Mars. Lake Karakul in Tajikistan, in the Eastern Pamir, is one example. We used ASTER and Landsat imagery for it. For the Moon, we took surface temperature data from LRO Diviner (especially the polar regions) and landing-area information from NASA’s Artemis III Candidate Landing Regions Report. For Mars, we used mineralogy and surface morphology data from the Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter (CRISM and HiRISE).

Data sources. We worked with open portals: NASA Earthdata Search, NASA Worldview, NASA Planetary Data System, the PDS Geosciences Node (LRO mission), ESA Open Science Data, and JAXA G-Portal. We also used Canadian Space Agency data (RCM and RADARSAT-1) and its tutorial on synthetic aperture radar. Images and articles about Karakul come from NASA Earth Observatory and NASA Photojournal (JPL).

Benefits. Scientists find a suitable place in one click instead of searching several sources, and the comparison with the Moon and Mars is right there. The information is simple and visual, so adults and children can both use the site. The bright visuals help children get interested in science.

Impact. The site speeds up the search for base testing sites. Anyone can use it, including schoolchildren.

Creativity. We combined scientific data from NASA, ESA, JAXA, and CSA with an interactive format. Instead of tables and long texts, users open places on a map and compare them with other planets themselves.

What we considered. We had two audiences in mind: specialists who need accuracy and speed, and children who need clarity and bright visuals. We also wanted the similarity between places to rest on satellite and orbiter data.
